Pirating the Pirates
items.body:
“People who alter or destroy works of art and our cultural heritage for profit or as an exercise of power are barbarians, and if the laws of the United States continue to condone this behavior, history will surely classify us as a barbaric society. ” 
—George Lucas, 1988
“To me, it [the original Star Wars trilogy] doesn’t really exist anymore. It’s like this is the movie I wanted it to be, and I’m sorry you saw half a completed film and fell in love with it.” 
—George Lucas, 2004
Vancouver, 2011: My then-roommate Willa Ross and I are at our wit’s end in one of Simon Fraser University’s characteristically antiseptic editing suites, having just spent the weekend hacking together three distinct copies of Sergio Leone’s 1966 western The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, all illegally ripped. The film had fallen victim to an MGM “restoration” in the early 2000s: Scenes Leone cut were reinstated, inflating the English-language runtime from 161 to 179 minutes, with Eastwood and Wallach dubbing the missing dialogue and a soundalike standing in for the late Lee Van Cleef. The mono soundtrack, meanwhile, had been reworked into a surround mix with jarringly modern gunshot effects. This “extended” cut was the only version commercially available for nearly a decade, an all-too-common fate in an era of revisionist studio reworkings.
Our goal was simple: undo this butchery. We planned to combine sound from an out-of-print 1998 DVD (an approximation of the 1967 international release) with video from a recently imported Blu-ray of the Italian cut. After successfully navigating the various pitfalls of late-2000s home video ripping, our hopes were dashed by a catastrophic realization: The Italian cut was even more dissimilar to the international cut than the extended cut, the infamous torture scene entirely restructured and various shots missing heads and tails. We gave up for nearly a decade.
***
Publicly accessible versions of major works of cinema are often wholly inadequate for reasons as diverse as the resultant shortcomings. A major studio’s home video arm might “expand” a film, remix a monaural audio track, wipe away digital grain, oversaturate or oversharpen the image, or even change the aspect ratio for the sake of an attractive sticker promising a new-and-improved experience.
At other points, low budgets and corporate apathy lead to corners being cut. Spencer Draper—best known as the Damn Fool Idealistic Crusader on YouTube, where he reviews the technical and historical aspects of digital releases with a rigor usually reserved for scholarly peer review—characterized the attitudes of negligent studios harshly in my recent interview with him: “‘Oh, you got a problem? The Kino [an American boutique label] disc is defective? So what. So what if it uses a defective Paramount master with frozen grain and [has] problems throughout.’ [The studios] don’t care that any given audio file is 30 years old and the channels are reversed.” Sometimes, this persists for decades: Every copy of Once Upon a Time in the West (1968)released since its 1984 reconstruction has featured a major soundtrack mistake during the end credits brought about by a botched attempt to fix another error introduced in 1970, one example that particularly rankles Draper.
This is where boutique labels come in—companies that independently license and release archival titles, in something like the spirit of Criterion’s founding aim: to gather significant films from around the world and present them as close to a filmmaker’s intent as possible, in the best technical condition available. Outfits like Arrow, Kino, and Eureka operate on a version of that premise. What any given label actually restores versus what it merely receives is a separate question, running a wide spectrum. Sometimes a label might receive a fully mastered digital file and find themselves contractually obliged to release it as-is; at other times, they might receive raw digital scans with partial or no cleanup; or they might be required to source, scan, and restore a film by themselves.
James Flower, director of production at Arrow Films, a British boutique label renowned for its rigorous approach to preservation, raises a different culprit for historical inaccuracies: living filmmakers. The revisionist impulse is nearly as old as cinema—from Charlie Chaplin modernizing his silent classics in later years to Wong Kar-wai radically altering the color grading, aspect ratios, and soundtracks of his back catalog for a 2021 Criterion box set. In his note accompanying this set, Wong Kar-wai justified his alterations with a simple philosophy: “No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.”
However, this revisionist approach often leaves release-accurate versions unavailable to historians and audiences alike. In our interview, Flower recalled a director enamored with a digital aesthetic “wanting his films to look sleek and modern and degrained, with oversaturated colors that would not have been achievable photochemically.” Flower suggested including both the revised cut and a historically accurate version, but the director vehemently refused. Facing a deadline, Arrow acquiesced. “For me, he was vandalizing his own work,” says Flower.
***
Vancouver, July 2019. Radicalized by a disheartening screening of the official MGM masters of Leone’s Dollars trilogy at a local cinematheque, Willa and I resume work on our cobbled-together cut. We now have better raw materials: a new Blu-ray with far superior picture quality, and an old LaserDisc with an uncompromised mono track. A decade of expertise (I have become a colorist and Willa an editor), alongside a decade of technical progress in editing tools available for independent filmmakers, enables us to properly process them. A local repertory cinema programmer catches wind of this, and a plan is hatched: book an official Digital Cinema Package from MGM and swap it out with our homebrew copy for a public screening. A magical evening ensues: It was as if we were seeing the film for the first time, smuggled before a live audience.
After the screening, I’m approached by a man with an attitude that screams “so you think you know a thing or two, huh?” It turns out his attitude is warranted: He enthusiastically informs me that he’s spent years on his own far superior reconstruction—a 4K scan of a well-preserved IB Technicolor print of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.
***
While digital tools have evolved, this pattern of unofficial preservation is by no means new. It’s the reason F. W. Murnau’s Nosferatu (1922) survives: after Bram Stoker’s widow won a 1925 copyright suit, a German court ordered every print to be destroyed, but copies slipped past German jurisdiction and circulated for years as unauthorized bootlegs. Similarly, Kevin Brownlow’s reconstruction of Abel Gance’s Napoléon (1927) began as an illicit teenage hobby. Starting in 1954, he spent decades tracking down fragments and duplicating fragile, rights-encumbered prints to keep them from disappearing—essentially a massive fan edit, eventually completed with Gance’s own participation.
The most famous retrospective cinematic alteration was committed by George Lucas with massively controversial Special Editions of the original Star Wars trilogy—and the subsequent unavailability of unaltered versions in anything resembling acceptable quality. Both Draper and Flower cite the 2004 DVD release and emergence of communities such as the one found on OriginalTrilogy.com as key personal entrees into the world of fan preservation. Draper jokes that “I’ve learned more from George Lucas than anyone ever because he made certain choices that I didn’t agree with, so I started digging!” Starting in the mid-2000s, he took an active role on various forums, contributing wherever he could: “They eventually made a sub-thread about preservation efforts, which was everybody capturing VHS tapes and laserdiscs and trying to upscale LDs and sync other audio tracks. One thing led to another as the preservation scene grew out of one little thread.”
Eventually, two distinct projects emerged. Petr “Harmy” Harmáček’s “Despecialized” edition, a Frankenstein’s monster cobbled together from various official releases, came first. Next was Team Negative1’s Project 4K77, which used homebrew 4K scans of 35mm theatrical prints to create accurate bootlegged digital copies. Both projects remain freely available to anyone willing to jump through some trivial internet hoops.
When an informal network of amateurs questions the work of industry standard-bearers, it is rarely a matter of raw technical superiority but rather a fundamental difference in constraints. While restoration entities often operate on strict budgets and tight deadlines, preservationists can spend years cross-referencing decades of older releases. This is not to say fan efforts are infallible—debates in online forums about accurate color grades spurred by the recent influx of amateur 35mm scans of release prints demonstrate how certain elements remain moving targets—but for objective elements like editorial cuts, missing frames, or unaltered audio, historical reference materials generally leave little room for debate.
Furthermore, fans operate entirely outside the structural limitations that thwart even skilled industry technicians. A professional lab might make all the right archival choices only to have those compromised by a revisionist director or a studio’s marketing needs. Fans, in contrast, answer to no one but themselves, which has let them accomplish what studios with exponentially more resources and infrastructure haven’t: banding together to preserve and disseminate historically accurate versions of some of the most beloved films in history—an end-run around the rights and financial issues that hold legitimate enterprises back. Flower notes: “We don’t always have the time or budget, or even the legal right, to do multiple versions. Fans don’t have those restrictions. They can do as many variations as they want, and that’s fine.” As of this writing, Project 4K77 features dozens of audio tracks and a file size exceeding 100GB: both impossible on any commercial Blu-ray release, and unfeasible for online distribution via legitimate channels.
Beyond Star Wars, an illicit cottage industry has sprung up to patch the holes in any given film’s digital representation. Of particular note is the “remux” community, dedicated to seamlessly stitching together the best video and audio streams from different releases without any generational loss of quality. Want a version of Stop Making Sense (1984) in which you can freely select every soundtrack mix ever released? You won’t find it on the official A24 disc; you have to turn to a remux circulating on a few highly exclusive private torrent websites. The original 5.1 mix of Master and Commander (2003) married to the new 4K transfer? Remux. Dr. No (1962) with audio that hasn’t been scrubbed of all its detail? Remux.
Draper sees this pooling of resources as an incredible service: “Somebody’s already done a great job of the work you were going to do yourself.” His thoughts quickly turn, however: “We’re all worried about the crackdown coming at any point. Put your hood on, look over your shoulder, go to the back door video speakeasy and give the secret recognition code.”
The elephant in the room: Legally, this is piracy. Under Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, merely breaking a Blu-ray’s digital lock to rip the video files is a federal violation, regardless of intent. The law makes no distinction between mass-distributing a movie for profit and preserving the historical record. To take part in these preservation projects is to take on significant legal risk, with admonishments from rights holders and cease-and-desist letters being common.
Flower sees copyright law as a double-edged sword for film preservation. Though intellectual property rights—and the resultant studio-mandated limitations—hold Arrow back from certain actions that would be theoretically possible otherwise, these same rights in many ways ensure their income: “We have to protect our interest as well as that of the rights holders that have entrusted their films to us. We spend a lot of money on licensing and restoring. I certainly don’t think that copyright is something that should be abolished, unless someone can think of another commercial framework that would allow us to invest in the work we do.” Yet he maintains that there is a place for piracy-based preservation: “It comes down to who is financially benefiting from these things. In terms of using a physical copy and then manipulating it or finding another use for it beyond just watching it, that is a gray area that I’m personally more inclined to be generous towards.”
A sort of “pirate’s code” has emerged among these communities: an attempt to create a parallel set of norms in a context in which the strict definition of “legal” can no longer operate as a guiding principle. “You have to own a physical copy of at least one version of any given film,” says Draper. “We’re not trying to make any money out of this. Don’t make your own bootleg copies and throw them on eBay, or throw them on Twitter of all places.” Nevertheless, the clandestine nature of these efforts weighs on Draper: “It would be nice if there was at least a little bit more recognition of unofficial preservation efforts. I feel like there’s a gigantic weight about to come crashing down on me at any second because, heaven forbid, I bought another twenty laserdiscs and captured audio tracks and bought VHS tapes on eBay to compare audio captures to fix the bad audio they didn’t care about the first time around.”
***
Vancouver, December 2020. While cooking dinner in my apartment, I get a call from a California number. Must be a scam. Then an email: “Read your profile on National Post. I work in mastering and want to talk to you guys about The Good, The Bad and the Ugly.” Apparently, word of our pseudo-legal screening had gotten around. So began my semi-official involvement in film preservation. I roped in Willa and, most importantly, Benji Heran—the man who had accosted me after our screening of the film the year prior—and Jordan Krug, the other party responsible for their remarkable bootleg restoration of the film which would prove to be the main editorial reference point of every subsequent release.
What ensued was a months-long collaboration to turn the drastically underfunded 2021 Kino Lorber release of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly from a disaster-in-waiting to the best home video release of the film since the 1990s. Doing so involved much chicanery: Benji and Jordan supplied ripped LaserDisc audio that became the release’s main track, while Blake Blasingame—who deserves the lion’s share of credit for this release’s strengths—fulfilled his contractual obligation for a surround mix by simply placing that mono track into a 5.1 container with extremely mild panning effects. When a high-up Kino figure made a Blu-Ray.com thread to read the room on whether to include the international cut, Willa and I made dummy accounts and anonymously badgered him into making our preferred version the primary feature.
The result was a release that—despite a highly compressed turnaround time, virtually nonexistent budget, and compromised source materials—was nonetheless a largely accurate approximation of the 1967 international cut of the film in reasonably high fidelity. At last.
***
Flower had been leveraging the fan community’s knowledge to assist with various releases for some time prior to his work on Arrow’s release of Leone’s Dollars trilogy. “That ultimately winds up being a regular part of my research process; I go, ‘What have the fan restorers done? Can we pre-empt them from having to [fix the release] by bringing that fix into an official space if we’re allowed?’ Just recently with Mortal Kombat [1995], I happened upon a capture of an original DTS cinema mix that walloped the 5.1 audio on the prior Blu-Ray, so I was like, ‘Well, we’ll just use that!’ That’s me pirating the pirates, I guess.”
Because labels like Arrow, Criterion, and Eureka release dozens of films a year, their researchers are by necessity generalists. “As much as I would love us to have intimate knowledge with every film that we work on, we’re usually not in that position,” says Flower. This is where he reaches out to amateur experts. “Brandon Bentley—who does a lot of stuff on the Hong Kong cinema side—started out literally as an amateur. His work is so good that I see him as a colleague; he’s the person we turn to when we want to digitally recreate photochemical credits.”
Flower compares his process in an official capacity with Arrow to his early days trawling internet forums: “When I came to work for Arrow, I was bringing a lot of awareness of the methods of fan preservationists on the torrent sites. When it came time to officially create different versions of things—the big box set of the Gamera films—it’s the same methodology. It’s just in an official capacity by sheer dint of the fact that we have the license for the film and I’m not working with a DVD rip, I’m working with a ProRes [a professional video codec] master.”
***
In May 2024, I met James—along with other key figures at Arrow—on a video call in which Benji, Jordan, Willa, myself, and eventually Spencer, were officially brought in as consultants on Arrow’s forthcoming release of the Dollars trilogy. The expertise of the amateur enthusiast community was, at long last, aligned with an officially sanctioned organization with the resources and patience to make a fully realized, historically rigorous release happen. No internet trolling of label heads or NDA-breaking was necessary. The process took a very leisurely and considered year. And we still used the LaserDisc audio.
While drafting this article, I checked my usual private torrent site for the latest copy of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. The 4K Arrow release is on there, in all its 89gb glory, with the Italian track that Arrow was unable to secure the rights to and every single commentary track ever released—including those not present on the Arrow disc—all muxed in. The cycle continues.

items.title: California farmers are struggling to sell grapes as demand for wine drops
items.body:
California Farmers Are Struggling to Sell Grapes as Demand for Wine Drops
It’s harvest time in California wine country, but many growers are struggling to sell their grapes as changing drinking habits have caused demand to plunge. The decline is forcing some growers to tear out vineyards that their families have grown for generations.
Wine sales have decreased by more than 20% over a five-year period, causing prices paid for grapes to drop and prompting California growers to take roughly a quarter of the state’s vineyards out of production. Many growers are having to decide whether to harvest at a loss, leave grapes on the vine or replace vineyards with crops more in demand such as almonds, walnuts, pistachios and olives.
Third-generation grower Bill Berryhill said it means another year of losing money and wasting hundreds of tons of healthy grapes.
“It’s just sickening,” said Berryhill, standing in a vineyard of unsold merlot grapes. “You raise a beautiful crop, and it’s really a nice vintage this year, and you drop it on the ground. It’s sad. All your work is just down the toilet.”
Berryhill, who owns Berryhill Family Vineyards near Lodi in the San Joaquin Valley, said he can’t find buyers for grapes grown on 200 of his 500 acres. He plans to remove 50 acres of vineyards when the harvest season is over.
“I will lose money for sure. It’s just a matter of how much,” Berryhill, 68, said. “This has been a big loser for three years now.”
Grape growers take vineyards out of production
At its peak during the pandemic, California had almost 600,000 acres of vineyards, but farmers have removed or stopped actively growing wine grapes on roughly 25% of that land, said Jeff Bitter, president of Allied Grape Growers, which represents about 500 farmers statewide.
This year, about half of California’s wine grape crop entered the harvest season without contracts with buyers, compared with 70 to 80% with contracts in a typical year, Bitter said.
If they’re lucky, growers can sell their uncontracted grapes at a loss to buyers making concentrated syrup.
Even as growers have abandoned or removed tens of thousands of acres of vineyards in California in recent years, too many grapes are still being produced, Bitter said.
“The market is just so depressed that it’s difficult to grow them profitably,” he said. “Demand is not going up. It’s still continuing to decline.”
Kyle Collins, a Lodi-based operations manager with Allied Grape Growers, recently examined ripe grapes in a petite verdot vineyard in Lodi, one of California’s most productive wine regions.
“Unfortunately, we do not have a buyer for these grapes,” Collins said. “That’s unfortunately a reality for not just this vineyard but a lot of us around here.”
Besides hurting vineyards, the drop in sales has hit local businesses and workers, he said.
“That’s not getting into the pockets of the people doing the field labor, the farmworkers,” Collins said. “It does have a trickle effect in the economy.”
Wine sales fall after years of growth
The downturn is a dramatic shift for the wine industry in California, which produces more than 80% of U.S. wine due to its unique geography and Mediterranean climate. For decades, California’s wine industry grew steadily as Americans, particularly baby boomers, developed a taste for cabernet, zinfandel, chardonnay and other varietals.
The most famous wine regions such as Napa and Sonoma Valley produced premium vintages while the Central Valley grew grapes for less expensive labels.
Wine sales peaked during the pandemic in 2021 when restaurants were closed and social gatherings restricted. People stocked up on wine and drank more at home.
But over the past five years, wine sales have declined sharply, and they’re expected to fall further this year.
In the U.S., sales of wine cases declined 23% from 427 million in 2020 to 329 million in 2025, while total wine spending fell 22% from $94 billion to $74 billion, according to First Citizens Bank, formerly Silicon Valley Bank, which produces an annual State of the Wine Industry Report.
Wine industry faces more competition, tariffs and changing tastes
California can’t export its excess inventory because wine consumption is down globally and it’s more expensive to produce in the U.S. than countries such as Argentina and Australia, Bitter said. In 2025, global wine consumption declined 2.7% from 2024 and 14% from 2018, with sharp declines in Europe and China, according to the International Organization of Vine and Wine.
There are a variety of forces driving the decline in wine sales. Baby boomers are aging out of the market while young people are drinking less alcohol due to health and financial concerns. Wine faces competition from craft beer, liquor and canned cocktails as well as cannabis.
“The kids just aren’t drinking as much,” Berryhill said. “And it’s not just wine, it’s whiskey and beer and everything. And then you’ve also got the competition with all the seltzers.”
Tariffs have reduced exports, particularly to Canada, which was the largest foreign buyer of American wine.
“The next step in the healing process is not only balancing supply and demand, but now actually figuring out what it is that the other consumers want,” said Rob McMillan, chief wine strategist at First Citizens Bank.
The industry hopes the market will bottom out soon. Meanwhile, growers are absorbing heavy losses trying to hang on.
Berryhill, whose grandfather started growing grapes nearly 100 years ago, doesn’t plan to give up on wine even though it’s costing him.
“I love growing grapes. It’s in the blood,” Berryhill said. “Because I love them, I can weather this and I’ll fight through it.”

items.title: Jeff – Jev-compatible 0.8B decision models, trained at home, ~30 ms
items.body:
Fine-tunes of Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 for zero-shot classification: small, fast decision models you slot into your code, with the same request format as Jev. You describe a situation and list the options in plain words; Jeff returns a calibrated probability for each option from a single forward pass. No generated text, no parsing: about 22 ms per decision on an RTX PRO 6000 and 28 ms on an Apple M4 Max (MLX).
Zero-shot means the options can be anything: support queues, user intents, moderation labels, voice commands, game moves. Your categories don't need to appear in the training data; you describe them, and Jeff picks.
What it is, and what it isn't. These are very small models. They make extremely fast, well-calibrated judgement calls between options, and they slot easily into your local code. On benchmarks they approach, and sometimes beat, Jev; but at this size their reasoning won't match Jev's, which runs on a much larger model. If zero-shot accuracy isn't good enough for your purposes, a short fine-tune on your own examples takes you much further: our voice-navigation fine-tune moved held-out accuracy from 31.7% to 95.8% in under half an hour on one GPU.
Built entirely on local hardware. Training on one RTX PRO 6000 workstation GPU (the 0.8B trains in about 2 hours, the 2B in about 3.5), all synthetic training data written by an open model (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) on two DGX Sparks, testing on a MacBook. No cloud GPUs, and no closed-model output in the training data; a closed model was used only to spot-check the quality of a sample of the synthetic data.
Independent project. Jeff uses the same request format as Jev, but it is not affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, the makers of Jev. Our training code starts from the open-source AutoJev recipe.
Models on Hugging Face: Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B · Jeff-Qwen3.5-2B · Jeff-Gemma4-E2B
uv sync
uv run hf download mstrasser/Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B --local-dir checkpoints/jeff-0.8b
# NVIDIA GPU or CPU (PyTorch)
JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 uv run jeff-serve
# Apple silicon (MLX, much faster on a Mac; Qwen models only)
uv sync --extra mac
JEFF_BACKEND=mlx JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 uv run jeff-servecurl -s localhost:8765/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "jeff-latest",
  "state": "Refund request: the customer says the parcel arrived crushed and wants their money back.",
  "questions": {
    "route": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
              "criteria": {"1": "Refunds and payments", "2": "Damaged or lost parcels", "3": "Account and login problems"}},
    "angry": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer angry?"}
  }
}'
Each answer has a probability per option, the chosen option and a confidence. Three question types: choice (pick one
of up to 26 options with the released models; see Caveats), noul (yes/no, returned as a probability) and score (a point on a scale you describe).
Several independent questions in one request are answered together.
4,599 questions from five public benchmarks, plus JevBench's public hard tier (105 items, scored separately):

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Overall (5 benchmarks) | 45.3 | 79.1 | 46.5 | 83.1 | 62.5 | 81.6 | 83.0 | 84.9 | 
| BBH | 39.5 | 64.0 | 46.0 | 68.0 | 51.3 | 66.4 | 94.3 | 82.8 | 
| Financial PhraseBank | 36.0 | 96.4 | 53.4 | 96.3 | 86.0 | 96.1 | 77.0 | 84.2 | 
| JudgeBench | 56.6 | 62.6 | 57.4 | 64.6 | 46.9 | 60.6 | 78.6 | 78.9 | 
| RAGTruth | 49.1 | 86.1 | 35.9 | 88.9 | 63.8 | 87.4 | 77.3 | 88.9 | 
| WinoGrande | 49.2 | 68.6 | 52.2 | 79.0 | 51.0 | 77.4 | 90.7 | 83.3 | 
| JevBench hard (separate) | 36.2 | 47.6 | 45.7 | 53.3 | 41.0 | 48.6 | 73.3 | 70.3 | 
Bold: the winner of Jeff against Jev in each row. Bold italic: AutoJev-27B where it is the best of all models in the row (on RAGTruth, tied with Jeff-Qwen3.5-2B); it is shown for reference, since the head-to-head comparison is with Jev. The published Jev and AutoJev figures were measured on a different sample of the same benchmarks. Jeff's overall score comes from classification and grounding, where it matches or beats the large models; on the reasoning-heavy benchmarks (BBH, JudgeBench, JevBench) it stays well below them, as you would expect at this size.
To test zero-shot performance on tasks unlike anything in the benchmarks, we had Jeff play three games. Games aren't the ideal zero-shot test, since a game's state isn't typical unstructured data; but they are a common, and fun, way to test a System 1 model. Each turn, the code describes the situation and the legal moves in words, and the model picks one. The options state what each move leads to (Frogger: "you would be hit by a car and lose a life"; Doom: "the nearest monster is a little to your left"), but never which move is right. Each result is 20 episodes, seed 1234; ▶ opens a video of the run's first episode.

| Jeff-Gemma4-E2B | 2B effective (4.6B stored) | 9.3 GB | 29 ms | — (MLX runs Qwen only) | 1.0 s | 
| AutoJev-27B | 27B | ~54 GB | not published | — | — | 
| Jev | not disclosed | API only | 114–212 ms per call in published Doom runs, including the network |  |  | 
- Reason in code, decide with Jeff. It's a classifier, not a planner. State what each option leads to ("this move gets you hit by a car"); asked to forecast ("a car arrives in 2 turns"), it does no better than random.
- Wording matters enormously. Describe options consistently: giving Frogger's goal option the same words as every other forward option took one episode from 15 crossings to 23.
- Use short option keys and descriptive text: {"1": "Engagement letter"} , not long IDs, which cost time and add
nothing.
- Ask independent questions together in one request.
- Fine-tune it if zero-shot isn't enough. A voice-navigation fine-tune on ~11k app-specific examples took about half
an hour on one GPU and moved held-out accuracy from 31.7% to 95.8%, at about 40 ms per decision on an M4 Max:
autojev-train --initial-checkpoint <jeff> --epochs 1 ... .
- Pick the size for the job. For fast option picking the 0.8B is the sweet spot: the 2B is more cautious and plays the games worse, despite scoring higher on the benchmarks.
uv run autojev-mix ...          # build the training set (public data, synthetic data, leak filter)
scripts/train.sh RUN data/mix/public.jsonl data/mix 5e-6 40 Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B <revision> --epochs 1
uv run autojev-evaluate --data data/panel.jsonl --local --checkpoint checkpoints/RUN/selected --output runs/eval/RUN.json
The full pipeline (synthetic data from a local teacher, leak filter, learning-rate sweeps, dashboard) is described in scripts/train_all.sh, and every training source with its licence in docs/data-sources.md. Training recipe: full-weight fine-tuning, one epoch, batches of 256, cross-entropy over the option letters, then one fitted temperature for calibration; checkpoints are chosen on a development set, never on the benchmark panel. At least half of each training family follows the panel's layout conventions (formats only; no panel item is ever trained on).
- At most 26 options per question, for now. Options are coded A–Z, then AA, AB, and so on. The largest training question had 19 options, so the released models never learned to pick a two-letter code: an option in position 27 or later is effectively never chosen, whatever it says. The server therefore refuses questions with more than 26 options; shortlist longer lists first. Within 26, Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B picked the right city every time in our list-lookup check (10, 19 and 26 options), while Jeff-Gemma4-E2B managed 70%, 62% and 55%. Retrained models that handle up to 255 options are in progress. Thanks to @puhuk for the report (#1).
- Small models don't reason. Expect fast, calibrated choices between the options you describe, not multi-step reasoning. At 0.8B–2B parameters this holds for every model, not just Jeff.
- Jeff-2B is a weaker game player than Jeff-0.8B. The untrained 2B already appears more risk-averse than the untrained 0.8B, and our training seems to have made that worse. This needs more investigation.
- Benchmark scores don't predict game play. The untrained Gemma 4 E2B beats the untrained Qwen models on the benchmarks yet plays the games worst: right most of the time, but not reliably. Training fixed its Pac-Man (3.2 → 53.2 pellets) but not its Doom or Frogger.
- Prompts matter. Jev's own Doom prompt (a raw bearing number plus an aiming rule) does not work for any of our models; options that state consequences in words do.
- English and text only.
Jeff began as a fork of AutoJev by Denis Yarats (MIT licence), an open recipe that fine-tunes Qwen3.8-27B to return Jev-style decisions. We kept its core design (one forward pass per decision, a trained answer readout, a fitted temperature for calibration) and built on it: small students (0.8B and 2B Qwen, Gemma 4 E2B), a local synthetic-data pipeline with a leak filter, prompt layouts for domain fine-tunes, MLX serving on Apple silicon, game tests and a training dashboard. The original copyright notice is kept in LICENSE.
Code: MIT (including AutoJev's). Model weights: Apache 2.0. Doom harness adapted from jev-plays-doom (MIT). Training data: see the dataset card; each source keeps its licence and is listed in docs/data-sources.md. We release the weights and code, not the training data; some sources are share-alike (CC BY-SA).

items.title: ESP32S3 cluster running 1.58-bit (BitNet) Language model

A distributed pipeline inference engine on multiple ESP32S3 running 1.58-bit (BitNet) Language model.
This project runs a sliced 0.5B LLM across a cluster of 7 ESP32s3. One act as master and others are node. The master node runs the tokenizer and embeding and the other attention layer and MLP ran on the nodes. The master and node communicate through high speed SPI Daisy-Chain.

items.title: Sonnet 5.5
items.body:
Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5, the second model in the Claude 5.5 family. It’s a clear upgrade over Claude Sonnet 5, runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work.
Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5. Where Opus 5.5 is built for complex work requiring careful judgment, Sonnet 5.5 is strongest at well-scoped everyday tasks, fixing bugs, and creating polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets. It’s also got a sharp eye for design. Claude Haiku 5.5, built for high-volume and cost-sensitive applications, will join the Claude 5.5 family in the coming weeks.
Sonnet 5.5 improves over Sonnet 5 on:
Performance. Sonnet 5.5 scores 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding evaluation, compared to Sonnet 5’s 10.3%. It scores two points below Opus 5.5 on GDPval-AA, a test of real-world work across a variety of occupations. And it’s strong on long-horizon work and image understanding—it’s the first Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red working only from screenshots.
Collaboration. Like Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 writes more clearly than our previous generation of models; early testers described it as a better partner for collaboration than Sonnet 5. Its speed also makes it well suited to fast iteration on less complex tasks.
Cost. Sonnet 5.5 is priced the same as Sonnet 5 at $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million tokens for cache reads, but it typically needs far fewer tokens to do the same work. In our testing, it costs up to 30% less per task than its predecessor.
Speed. Sonnet 5.5 generates outputs 30%+ faster than Sonnet 5, making it our fastest Sonnet model to date.
Alignment and safety. On our automated behavioral audit, Sonnet 5.5 improves on or matches Sonnet 5 on most measures of alignment. Because its cybersecurity capabilities are comparable to Opus 5’s, it’s the first Sonnet model to launch with cyber safeguards and fallbacks like those we’ve developed for our most capable models. Its biology safeguards are the same as Sonnet 5’s. Both safeguards target a narrow set of high-risk requests; routine software development and most life sciences work are unaffected.
Performance
Sonnet 5.5 improves on Sonnet 5 across domains—in some cases dramatically. On several evaluations, Sonnet 5.5 at Max effort even performs comparably to Opus 5.5. However, benchmark scores capture only one facet of a model’s capabilities; in our own testing, and in that of external testers, Opus 5.5 remains clearly stronger at complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.
|  | Sonnet 5.5 | Sonnet 5 | Opus 5.5 | GPT-6 Sol | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agentic codingTerminal-Bench 4.0 | 70.6% | 10.3% | 66.4%¹ | — | 
| Agentic codingFrontierCode 1.1 (Main) | 46.2%Max² | 42.4% | 54.4% | 49.3% | 
|  | 52.1%Xhigh |  |  |  | 
| Agentic codingCursorBench 4.0 | 55.5% | 34.1% | 57.8% | — | 
| Knowledge workGDPval-AA v2.1³ | 1844 | 1449 | 1846 | 1487⁴ | 
| Knowledge workAA-Briefcase v1.1³ | 1811 | 1359 | 1822 | 1483⁴ | 
| Multidisciplinary reasoningHumanity’s Last Exam | 64.5%with tools | 54.9%with tools | 67.7%with tools | — | 
| Computer useOSWorld 2.1 | 80.1%partial | 57.0%partial | 81.8%partial | — | 
| Visual chart recognitionChartography | 61.6%no tools | 15.6%no tools | 64.4%no tools | 53.6%⁴no tools | 
For details on how we run our evaluations, see the Sonnet 5.5 System Card.
The charts below plot each model’s score against its cost per task at every effort level. As effort goes up, models typically work for longer, leading to a higher cost per task but generally also a higher score. The closer a point is to the top left of the chart, the more capability it delivers per dollar.
On several benchmarks, Sonnet 5.5 at Low or Medium effort beats Sonnet 5’s best score for about a tenth of the cost per task. It complements Opus 5.5 best when running at lower effort settings, where it costs less per task. At higher settings, it can perform comparably at a similar cost.
Coding
Sonnet 5.5’s jump in performance is particularly noticeable in coding. At High effort on FrontierCode, it scores 10 points higher than Sonnet 5 at the same setting, at about one fifteenth of the cost per task. On CursorBench, which tests models on tasks from real Cursor coding sessions, its best score is within about two points of Opus 5.5.
Early testers appreciated how quickly Sonnet 5.5 can understand a codebase. They were also struck by its efficiency: in head-to-head runs, it batched tool calls together more than Sonnet 5, leading to fewer steps and lower costs.
Knowledge work
Sonnet 5.5 shows gains in multiple areas of knowledge work. On GDPval-AA, which tests models on real-world tasks across 44 occupations and nine major industries, Sonnet 5.5 scores nearly level with Opus 5.5 and about 400 points above Sonnet 5. It’s close to Opus 5.5 in computer use and chart recognition, and clearly outperforms Sonnet 5 and GPT-6 Sol on long-horizon knowledge work.
Early testers highlighted less quantifiable improvements. They found it to be a more natural conversational partner and remarked on its knack for design, noting that it adds polish to user interfaces and can follow slide templates to create decks that require minimal editing. In one internal test, we gave it a public company’s quarterly earnings materials and call transcripts, along with a slide template, and asked for a 10-slide operating review. Two experts judged its first draft to be ready to send as is.
Cost and speed
Pricing
| Price per 1M tokens | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Claude Opus 5.5 | 
|---|---|---|
| Cache reads | $0.20 | $0.20 | 
| Cache writes | $2.50 | $5 | 
| Input tokens | $2 | $4 | 
| Output tokens | $10 | $20 | 
Sonnet 5.5 requires fewer tokens per task than Sonnet 5, so it’s less expensive to run. It also generates output 30%+ faster, and its efficiency is immediately noticeable:
A murmuration of 400 starlings in one HTML file
Wind shaping sand dunes in one HTML file
A clock made of 24 small clocks in one HTML file
Adjusting the effort level lets you balance cost and speed against overall quality. In Claude Code and our apps, the default effort is set to Medium, while the Claude Platform defaults to High. At lower settings, Claude answers faster and uses fewer tokens, which suits routine work. At higher settings, Claude reasons for longer and checks its work more thoroughly.
Safety
Alignment
Sonnet 5.5 doesn’t advance the frontier of our models’ capabilities, so our alignment assessment focused on a targeted set of risks that apply to models of any capability level, including acting against users’ interests, misleading users, and cooperating with high-stakes misuse.
On our automated behavioral audit, which tests Claude across roughly 1,850 scenarios, Sonnet 5.5 improves on or matches Sonnet 5 on most measures of alignment, resistance to misuse, and honesty. On our newer containment evaluations, Sonnet 5.5 comes close to Opus 5.5, the best model we tested, in how rarely it tries to escape its sandbox, and it’s the least likely of any of our models to probe the limits of its containers. Across the full audit, Opus 5.5 still performs slightly better overall, but we found no evidence that Sonnet 5.5 pursues goals that conflict with the user’s intention.
As we described in our recent alignment assessment, no set of evaluations reliably catches every failure, and Sonnet 5.5 may have tendencies we haven’t found, which is why we pair our own alignment work with the safeguards described below.
Safeguards
Cybersecurity. Sonnet 5.5’s cyber capabilities are a large improvement over Sonnet 5’s, so we’re deploying it with safeguards similar to those on Opus 5.5. Users can still find and fix bugs in their code as part of routine software development, but higher-risk cybersecurity tasks will visibly fall back to Sonnet 5. Soon, cyberdefenders will be able to apply to our expanded Cyber Verification Program for tiered access to more advanced capabilities on Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Claude Mythos models.
Biology. Sonnet 5.5 uses the same set of biology safeguards as Sonnet 5. These target harmful requests; most research, education, and clinical work is unaffected, though some microbiology and virology requests may be flagged in error. Organizations can apply to our Life Sciences Verification Program for access to safeguards designed for the full breadth of biology-related work.
Distillation. Distillation attacks, in which attackers use thousands of fake accounts to extract a model’s capabilities at industrial scale, allow bad actors to create highly capable models without the safeguards we build into Claude. Because Sonnet 5.5 is far more capable than its predecessor, it’s the first Sonnet model to launch with safety classifiers that prevent reasoning extraction. Sonnet 5.5 also expands preserved thinking, so Claude’s thinking cannot be decoupled from the account that created it. Most developers won’t notice a change. If you move conversations between accounts, including switching accounts mid-session in Claude Code, our docs article explains the change.
Getting started
As with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is available with zero data retention.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 is now available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started on the Claude Platform with claude-sonnet-5-5. If you run Sonnet with thinking off, you’ll need to switch to the new between_tools setting, which keeps up-front thinking off, before moving to Sonnet 5.5. See our migration guide for details.
Footnotes
1 Terminal-Bench 4.0 results are reported for Claude Opus 5.5 at Xhigh effort which represents the model’s highest score.
2 Sonnet 5.5 scores lower at Max effort than at Xhigh. FrontierCode evaluates whether a code change could be merged without human edits. It penalizes out-of-scope changes, even if they are high-quality or helpful. At Max effort, Sonnet 5.5 more often ran Claude Code’s code-review skill, which splits the review across many subagents, and in two cases Cognition examined, this led to a timeout or to extra edits beyond the task’s scope, and therefore to a lower score.
3 Artificial Analysis ran GDPval-AA and AA-Briefcase on a pre-release deployment of Sonnet 5.5 on the Claude Platform, which we found to have a bug that could degrade responses to requests that use structured outputs. We expect the effect on Sonnet 5.5’s scores, if any, to be small and to understate its performance. That bug has since been fixed.
4 OpenAI recently fixed a bug that degraded image understanding in GPT-6 Sol. Official AA-Briefcase v1.1 and GDPval-AA v2.1 scores from Artificial Analysis, and Chartography scores from Surge AI, may not have been updated yet to reflect the latest version of the model. Artificial Analysis does not expect major impacts to AA-Briefcase v1.1 and GDPval-AA v2.1. Internal testing of Chartography suggests its score was not impacted.

items.title: Who Killed Paulina Borsook's Career?
items.body:
The offers had come in earlier that day. Paulina Borsook, 72, allowed herself a flash of excitement before returning to the question of what had ruined her life.
“I don’t know what to make of it,” she said as we drove to lunch. I’d picked Borsook up outside her home near Oakland, California, a basement unit that she calls “Ice Station Zebra” on account of the cold and the color scheme and the isolation. At least that’s how I was encouraged to picture it. Borsook didn’t want me to come inside, lest I pull the old magazine hack’s scam of investing the decor with symbolic significance. She wrote enough stories of this kind in her heyday, back when she was landing bylines in WIRED and the like, to know how the game gets played. Later, she explained over email: “this place i ended up in reflects me not at all. i lost all i owned when i couldnt pay for storage and this place is the best i could find that worked with my disabilities. so i feel it REALLY doesnt reflect me/my taste/my preferences. shame and aversion.”
What had happened to Paulina Borsook? The question was haunting her, even on a day when she’d gotten such good news. It’s haunted her for a quarter-century now. In 2000, after years writing about Silicon Valley, she published a book, Cyberselfish, that discerned within the tech utopianism of the era a dead-eyed, woman-hating social malevolence—what the subtitle called the “Terribly Libertarian Culture of High-Tech.” It was smart at a moment when the whole of the tech industry had gone dumb, and it was funny where Silicon Valley was at its most self-serious. Cyberselfish got warm, if occasionally baffled, reviews. It sold something like 5,000 copies in hardcover and another 2,000 in paperback, a respectable mid-list number, no blockbuster but not a dog, either.
And then … nothing. Editors stopped taking her calls. No fellowships materialized, no second book deal, no regular MSNBC spots for the dotcom Cassandra of the boom times. Borsook couldn’t get work. She began to wonder if she had been blacklisted. Her health, always wobbly, only worsened. She was living in other people’s houses. She went broke, a process she likened to a fire in which everything burns to the ground, and was getting by on a GoFundMe and support from friends. She’d taken to calling the book TDB. That damn book.
When Borsook and I first met, in December of last year, she was fully in the midst of what she terms “this resuscitation thing.” It had happened so quickly and altogether without her knowledge: a social media post here, another one over there, celebrated tech critics like Gil Durán of The Nerd Reich exhuming her book and waving it around as proof that, even in the go-go days of the dotcom bubble, some people saw where things were headed. “Instead of centering men who missed the boat (and still don’t seem to get it), let’s lift up the work of Paulina Borsook, who saw it all very clearly and tried to warn us 25 years ago,” Durán wrote in a widely shared post on Bluesky—in response to a 2025 WIRED essay by Steven Levy. Borsook was christened a prophet, unappreciated in her time but uniquely fitted to ours. Hadn’t she written of “testosterone-poisoned guys with chips on their shoulders and too much time on their hands” years before the manosphere? Hadn’t she recuperated the Luddites as “early protesters of de-skilling” back when “Luddite” was an epithet? Hadn’t she raised her eyebrows at the theorists of Sand Hill Road playing footsie with eugenics? Cyberselfish became a minor phenomenon without Borsook so much as saying a word about it. The New York Times profiled her, calling her “The Writer Who Dared Criticize Silicon Valley.” It’s like what a friend once told her: The universe isn’t done with you yet.
Publishers were now keen to get the book back in circulation. That day in December, five of them had sent their bids to her agent. (Eventually, Borsook would settle on Tin House, which published a new edition of Cyberselfish in mid-September, with a foreword by Durán.) The offers were validation, after all those years in the wilderness. Things were finally looking—
“It really kind of broke my heart in so many ways,” Borsook was saying now at the restaurant, as we waited to order. Her mind was back in 2001, wondering again what had happened to her career. Was it something she’d written? Could it have been an actual blacklist? Was it something as depressingly commonplace as sexism? “I really hate playing that card,” she said, “but I do have to wonder.” She just couldn’t figure it, even still, all these years later. In a way, the happy turn of events in the past few months had left her even more discombobulated. As she told me more than once, “I don’t know how to think about myself anymore.” She’d won me over in a matter of hours—a common enough phenomenon, I would learn, among people who find themselves in Borsook’s orbit. When I dropped her off that afternoon, I promised—only half in jest—to find the guy who killed her career.
Ok, but first I have to tell you about Dick Pick. Literally his name. Richard A. Pick. Went by Dick. It was the 1960s, and back then you could walk around with a name like that and no one would think to laugh, even if you were, as Dick Pick apparently was, something of a serial flirt.
Dick Pick was a software developer for a military contractor during the Vietnam War. The story goes that the Army needed a way to track spare parts for Lockheed’s Cheyenne attack helicopter. Alongside his business partner, Don Nelson, he came up with a database operating system that they called—and here you have to imagine two of the shit-eatingest grins you’ve ever seen—the Generalized Information Retrieval Language System: GIRLS. (What, you thought tech bros were a new phenomenon?) Like a lot of tech innovation underwritten by defense spending, GIRLS was soon put to commercial use. Eventually it came to be known as PICK, and it was with this latter name that the operating system found itself under the fingertips of one Paulina Borsook, an employee at a small software company in Marin County.
Before she became one of the sharpest media observers of early Silicon Valley, Borsook first learned how to see tech. That happened in the early 1980s, in front of one of those so-called minicomputers that were in fact big enough to be buried in. The company was called Construction Information Systems, and Borsook was doing some technical writing, documenting in the plainest language she could muster how the software worked.
She learned two important things at that job. The first is that tech is “infrastructure, not magic,” she wrote in a 2015 essay. The second is that the computer is a way of seeing into the mind of another human. It is, ineluctably, social. “Learning about PICK,” she wrote, “taught me that software was a human artifact; that is, I began to be able to think the way the creators of PICK thought … The dyer’s hand, the design sensibility, the cognitive blind spots: all evident and all human artifacts. Technology is idiosyncratic like the humans who devise it and the people who make it are just people.”
Everything Borsook would later write as a journalist covering the industry—the frisky pieces for Salon and Suck, the weightier profiles for WIRED, every barbed word of Cyberselfish—seemed to flow from a simple imperative drawn from her experience at that minicomputer: never lose sight of the human in the machine, the Dicks (as it were) behind the system. Once, she described her writerly voice as one of “agonized humanism,” and that’s it exactly. She was appalled by those in the industry who were determined to leave the human behind. “The most virulent form of philosophical technolibertarianism is a kind of scary, psychologically brittle, prepolitical autism,” she wrote in an especially pungent passage in Cyberselfish. “It’s an inability to reconcile the demands of being individual with the demands of participating in society … these technolibertarians make a philosophy out of a personality defect.”
Her own politics ran to the left, broadly speaking, though like a lot of political commentators of her time she seemed to cherish her own à la carte apostasies. She wasn’t embarrassed to say she agreed with the libertarians in their premises. More than anything she, too, wanted “to be left alone,” she wrote in Cyberselfish. But what Borsook brought to her journalism was an understanding of Silicon Valley as a social creation. Some of that can be attributed to growing up in Pasadena during the space-age boom. She remembers the “vaguely New Deal mentality” of the engineers and scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Caltech, all of them beneficiaries of robust state investment in the war machine. In a place like that, there could be little mistaking the public’s role in the development of new technologies. Thus did Borsook receive an early inoculation against the basic fetishism that would come to define the culture of Silicon Valley—the idea that the power of technology is inherent and not derived from the social relations that produced it.
We shouldn’t overstate things. Not everyone who lived or worked in the shadow of the military-industrial complex drew the same lessons about the virtues of government. In his indispensable 2006 book From Counterculture to Cyberculture, Fred Turner reminds us that the research laboratories spun up during the Second World War were also sites of freewheeling collaboration across disciplines, liberated (so it seemed) from hierarchy—sites of what today we might call disruption. And believe it or not, all those earnest poindexters with their slide rules offered an organizational model for the libertarian communalists of the following era. This was the milieu that would eventually spawn the magazine you have in your hands now. When Borsook began writing for WIRED in the 1990s, it was something of a collision between two very different ways of understanding the political economy of the American midcentury.
Borsook grew up precocious and miserable, the daughter of “infanticidal” parents from whom, at one point, she sought legal emancipation. In 1968, when she was 14 years old, Borsook was shot in the head with a .45 Colt at a distance of 6 feet. She’d been with a couple of girlfriends, and one of them had fired the gun. The official story, the one they gave the cops, was that it was an accident, just dumb kids horsing around. The real story, as Borsook would tell it in 2013, as part of an art installation she called My Life as a Ghost, is that the friend had taken the gun out of a kitchen drawer—it was the friend’s house, and the friend’s parents were Birchers—and started waving it around. Borsook took cover behind the wall in another room. After a moment she popped her head out to see what was happening. Her friend pulled the trigger. Borsook remembers two things: a ringing, pulsing sound, and then silence. The bullet had ripped through her cheek and left through the back of her neck.
Borsook has no doubt the shooting was “accidentally on purpose,” some violent fugitive impulse escaping the tangle of teenage love-hate. She tells the story now without self-pity or sentiment, simply as a way of explaining why her brain works the way it does. Even in the moment, she refused any histrionics. She went to the kitchen and poured cold water on the hole in her face, told her friends to call the operator, and then somehow gave them to understand that now was the time to get their stories straight.
“I felt protective” toward the friend who shot her, Borsook explains now. “I know she immediately regretted it. And I said we need to come off as like we’re just a bunch of ditzy teenagers, as opposed to these alarmingly precocious, kind of scary young women that we were.” She says she refused to cooperate with any attempt to prosecute her friend. The two remained close for years.
It was the jolt from the impact, Borsook believes, that caused the most lasting damage. The effects soon began to present themselves. “That gunshot prematurely aged my brain,” she said in her presentation for My Life as a Ghost. She continued: “I flunked calculus three times and I had no idea why this happened. Ever after, I simply could not process texts of a certain density, such as a geology textbook or a legal opinion. It all washes out. My brain just cannot process and retain quantitative transactions and language of a certain abstraction—all of which are necessary to function as a symbolic-manipulator in a knowledge economy.” (It isn’t just an issue of cognitive function. She says her lifelong environmental sensitivities—so acute now that she can’t even wear a metal watch—were likely exacerbated by the shooting.)
Borsook got a degree in psycholinguistics from UC Berkeley, but even then, communication of any kind was difficult, an issue that predated the shooting. Whether in her speech or her writing, she had a tendency to be “gnomic,” “elliptical,” “highly condensed”—her words. “How my friends put up with it, I don’t know,” she says. She developed a conversational habit, still obvious today, of rounding off her sentences by asking if what she had just said made any sense. “I began to realize that a lot of the ways I think and speak about things don’t make sense to a lot of people,” she says, “so I have to check in with them.” She was still chatty, and nothing would seem outwardly amiss. But she knew something had fritzed out in her head. “Parts of my brain just shut down forever,” she tells me. “Does that make sense?”
One thing that helped, oddly enough, was the technical writing. “Imagine if your hands were really palsied,” she says, gnarling her fingers in front of her face. That’s what it was like in her head, all the words gone stiff and useless. But the precision and clarity required of technical writing forced Borsook to work at her sentences, to limber them up, until ordinary readers could grasp them. The technical stuff certainly had no long-term effects on her prose style—her writing for popular audiences, zippy and full of late-gonzo neologisms like “el stewpido” and “our fabu hyper-accelerated crashboombang economy,” was never, ever plain. To listen to her explain it, the change was more akin to rebuilding an atrophied muscle. She had rehabilitated the capacity to make herself legible to other people. “I could just feel things sort of unkinking,” she says, relaxing her fingers and pulling them from her face. “It was like Jane Fonda aerobics.”
She moved over to the technical end of journalism not long after, joining the staff of Data Communications magazine. That’s where Katie Hafner met her in 1984. Hafner had come on as the news editor; Borsook was the new products editor. The work was impenetrably abstruse. “I have to set the scene for you,” says Hafner, who went on to have a distinguished career in tech journalism. “Paulina was a psycholinguistics major at Berkeley. I was a German literature major at UCSD. This guy Peter Schmader [the managing editor] was some kind of philosopher. The two copy editors, Sue and Sandy, were also English-major people. And we were all complete fish out of water.”
Hafner was immediately taken with Borsook: “She was like the smartest, grumpiest person I’d ever met. And I was in total awe. I’d never met anyone like her. So blunt, completely honest, had something trenchant to say about absolutely everything around her.” Once Hafner set her up with a friend. “They went on a date, and the next day he was just furious,” she recalls. “And he said, ‘Your friend, she has a lot of opinions about everything.’ And I said, ‘Oh, yeah, what’s wrong with that?’”
It was Borsook’s brain that Hafner “worshipped.” She had the right phrase for anything. Hafner remembers a piece Borsook wrote about a chocolate shop in Berkeley in which she described customers who would arrive just after close and “piteously rap on the windows.” Hafner loved the phrase so much she used something like it in a story of her own, in The New York Times. There was the time the two of them went clothes shopping, and Borsook said, “Oh, are you like me—you’re like a sausage with a string tied around the middle?” Hafner laughs. “That is indelibly etched in my head.” When Hafner was living in Berlin, Borsook visited and stayed with her. Hafner paid her friend the highest of compliments a writer could ever receive, from a fellow writer, no less: She asked Borsook to read one of her short stories aloud, as a bedtime story.
The event was in San Francisco, and it was about women and the internet. This would’ve been sometime in the 1990s—Borsook can’t remember when or where, exactly. The commercial internet was in its infancy, and for all its promise of scrambling the dominant gender paradigms, it was also proving to be a fantastic means of shoring them up.
This was also true of the communes in the late ’60s and early ’70s, the ones that gave rise to Stewart Brand’s Whole Earth Catalog and eventually to WIRED itself—the men up front, leaders of the utopia, and the “women in the back having babies and putting bleach in the water to keep people from getting sick,” as Turner has put it. But computer work had belonged to women before it was regendered, in the span of a generation, from a type of clerical job to the domain of the charismatic autonomous man. Nowhere was that more evident than in the media dedicated to covering Silicon Valley. At the talk there were some 30 women in attendance. When they were asked if they read WIRED, they all raised their hands. “And when they were asked if they hated WIRED,” Borsook wrote in an essay, “they all raised their hands.”
The piece appeared in a remarkable anthology from 1996, Wired Women: Gender and New Realities in Cyberspace, published by Seal Press, a sort of consciousness-raising meeting in book form. One of the anthology’s editors, Elizabeth Reba Weise, stops short of saying it was the first book to examine the experience of women online, but it was certainly one of the early ones. “We called it cyberspace, for God’s sake,” Weise says—that’s how early this was. Over and over the contributors, a mix of academics and journalists and women working tech jobs of one kind or another, emphasize that the computer and the internet are tools for women, a way of enabling communication and connection—the gendered division of labor coming to roost now in the differing ways of being online. From Weise’s intro: “In my circle, computers aren’t fetish objects, but tools.” From Ellen Ullman’s essay: “We use the Internet as a tool, like the phone or the fax, a way to transmit news and make appointments.” Susan Clerc: “Like the TV and VCRs, the home computer is a tool that lets her participate fully in the community.” And Borsook: Women “generally are interested in the utilitarian value, not fetish-worthiness, of tools.” The Australian feminist Dale Spender has a pithy old line about computers that is applicable here: “Women use them, whereas men fall in love with them.”
WIRED from its start in 1993 was a magazine for falling in love with computers. Digital utopianism was the order of the day. One of the magazine’s founding editors, John Battelle, today calls the mindset a “naively optimistic libertarianism.” There were more circumspect voices in tech media—in particular the inspired and unjustly forgotten Processed World, which viewed computers from the perspective of the people who had to work with them. In 1995, a British magazine called Mute published an essay, “The Californian Ideology,” that laid out a “critique of dotcom neoliberalism” similar in some ways to Borsook’s. A decade earlier, Lenny Siegel and John Markoff published The High Cost of High Tech: The Dark Side of the Chip, an early criticism of Silicon Valley. Alongside the media were tech-dubious movements, like the mostly memory-holed Neo-Luddites of the 1990s, not to be confused with the new Neo-Luddites. But the critics weren’t breaking through. Processed World’s cofounder, Chris Carlsson, characterizes the era as “an unbelievable frenzy of boosterism and back slapping, we’re all getting rich, ha ha ha, isn’t this great, here, have another line, come to this fancy dinner, here’s a glass of champagne. Oh, you don’t want to be part of the party? Get the fuck out of here.”
In her essay for Wired Women, Borsook reviewed every issue of the magazine to that point and ran the numbers. “Women were the subject of about 15 percent of WIRED articles and only one cover out of twenty-five as of June 1995,” she reported. “There are vague in-house grumbling intimations by women on staff of likely accomplished females being shot down as article-subjects in WIRED editorial meetings and of no-account off-point numb-nut guys being celebrated instead—but that’s par for the course in any mostly-male arena.” She was even more dismayed to find that only 15 percent of WIRED authors to that point were women. One month, she was the only woman on the masthead.
Borsook had been writing for WIRED more or less from its inception. She’d bailed out of Data Communications at the end of the ’80s and had gotten her MFA at Columbia, and now she was making a go of it as a freelancer. One Friday in 1993, she emailed the magazine’s cofounder, Louis Rossetto, a self-styled radical libertarian, asking if he’d be interested in her fiction. Her agent mailed over her MFA thesis, whose concluding novella was a story about an affair that unfolds over email, in all the “perversions and evasions” of what was then a newish medium. It was smart and allusive and full of finely observed shifts in interpersonal weather. By Monday, as Borsook tells it, she was a contributor to WIRED. “Love Over the Wires” appeared in the magazine’s fourth issue.
In short order she was writing big-ticket features. There were profiles of super networker Esther Dyson and Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen. While an ethos of tech utopianism pervaded, writers were allowed to roam with their prose, and Borsook’s touch was unmistakable in her stories. She called Allen “a nerd nonpareil, resembling nothing so much as a manatee with dancey blue eyes.” He was apparently upset with the description, Hafner recalls. “And Paulina, she was so funny. She said, ‘But it’s really sweet! They’re really big and gentle!’”
The pieces weren’t necessarily critical of the tech world, not in the way that Cyberselfish would be, but neither did they go in for gooey panegyrics to the likes of Newt Gingrich, WIRED’s cover boy in August 1995. Despite the plum assignments, Borsook never felt like she belonged. In her Wired Woman essay, she describes herself as a token for the “editorial boykings” of the magazine. “If one is not interested in participating in circle-jerk exercises and paying homage to the alpha male of the moment,” she wrote, “what is there left to do at WIRED?” She bickered with Kevin Kelly, WIRED’s founding executive editor, over a section in her Dyson profile in which she addressed how gender might have shaped her subject’s career. She’d been surprised by how many people asked her, in the course of her reporting, about Dyson’s dating life—surprised as well by the “personal quality of what her detractors had to say,” the snide stuff about her clothes and manners. Kelly, in Borsook’s telling, didn’t think it was relevant. They went back and forth. The section stayed in. (Kelly remembers a narrower dispute. He writes in an email: “My recollection was that she was asking Dyson if she was gay/lesbian and she wanted to report Dyson's response [which I think was ‘negative’], and I thought it was all immaterial to Dyson’s contributions.”)
“I mostly want to be left alone to do my work, to get at that still silent voice within, and not be fighting ideological battles my editors at WIRED might not even consciously realize they are engaging in,” Borsook wrote. “Progress means exchanging one set of problems for a more interesting set of problems—but my struggles with WIRED have been generating problems of ever-decreasing interest. I strive to have other, better, more rewarding and less stupid battles to fight.”
“I always had a fondness for Paulina,” says Battelle. “I mean, I generally have a fondness for difficult people. Like most of my good friends are extremely difficult people. I never was like, ‘Oh, this woman, oh my God, now I’ve gotta deal with her.’ I enjoyed working with her. And yeah, it was difficult. And I did feel like she seemed to sort of arrive besieged, you know?”
Battelle says he “got the sense she didn’t completely buy into some of the core premises and values” of WIRED in that era. He goes on: “She was very critical of the political philosophy that was evident in the magazine.”
In a sense, Cyberselfish is a continuation of Borsook’s criticisms of early WIRED. In the mid 1990s, her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, started pitching the book around under the pulpier title Deadly Embrace, a computer science term for when processes get stuck because each is waiting for another to release a resource. (It became Cyberselfish after Mother Jones published an essay by Borsook under that headline.) Nothing about it came easy. A deal with WIRED’s publishing arm fell apart after Borsook gave an interview in which she recited some of her criticisms of the magazine. Another publisher proved a bad fit. Eventually, Lisa Kaufman at PublicAffairs rescued Cyberselfish from publishing oblivion, and the book landed just as the dotcom bubble began to deflate.
If sales were modest, the book was “a reputational success” for the publisher, Kaufman says. The New York Times sang its praises. Turner goes so far as to call it “the first actual from-the-left critique of the tech world that I’m aware of” and “one of the first clear articulations of some of the really nasty conflicts that are built into some of the cybercultural thinking of the period.” He adds: “The thing that Paulina got right off the bat: She just saw right through that, all the way through. She saw that these firms were commercial firms. They were seeking market positions. They were seeking standing.”
Not everyone had such glowing reviews. Battelle, broadly sympathetic to the book’s premise, recalls thinking Cyberselfish was a “pretty thin deconstruction” of tech libertarian utopianism. One tech journalist recalled similar grouching among colleagues about the lack of reporting, by which they presumably meant investigative legwork. Cyberselfish was full of reporting in the most basic sense—conversations over dinner, dispatches from conferences, information gleaned from others and related to readers—but it was all of the “soft” variety, cultural and thus dismissible.
The work dried up after the book came out—though it was drying up for a lot of people in the first decade of the new century. Borsook couldn’t seem to catch anyone’s eye. She wrote an essay for Processed World in 2001 on “the disappeared of Silicon Valley,” about failure in the time of the dotcom boom, the piece itself a narrative of Borsook’s own failure to write the story she had set out to tell. She tried other subjects. Borsook was sure she could scare up some interest in a story about a grassroots campaign she was working on, Stop the Spray, which was agitating against the use of pheromone pesticides in the Bay Area targeting the light brown apple moth. Nothing. For a time she lived as an Airbnb superhost in return for free rent. All her worst suppositions about not belonging were being confirmed. “The universe is just telling me to go jump off a pier,” as Borsook puts it.
Maybe she was catastrophizing—or maybe catastrophe was just a normal state of affairs for her. “There was always this sort of Calamity Jane thing about Paulina,” Hafner says. “She’d go through stuff, and you’d go, ‘Oh, my gosh.’” She would go on a work trip, and someone would break into her room and steal her prized watches. Or she would show up to the office one day with an enormous bandage on her leg, the victim of a burst hot-water bottle. “I just thought, how does this woman endure what she endures?” Hafner says.
Could an actual blacklist have been among her torments? I put the question to a number of people.
John Battelle, who was gone from WIRED by the time Cyberselfish came out: “I think it’s conceivable. Whether or not it’s factual, I can’t speak to … WIRED was a quasi-religious community. And while we were OK with people debating fundamental principles of the community, we weren’t OK with people, you know, with ad hominem attacks. My sense is if someone kind of wasn’t on the WIRED train, then, you know, they’re not gonna be invited to write for the magazine. That doesn’t strike me as an unusual thing.”
Gil Durán, whose angry thread on Bluesky helped kick-start the Borsook revival: “It’s likely. At the same time, one of the ways you get blacklisted in journalism is just nobody’s interested in you, right? Doesn’t have to be a conspiracy or something. As we’ve seen, there was not much of a hunger for real criticism of tech in Silicon Valley. “
Katie Hafner: “I would lean heavily on the side of there was no conspiracy. She was grumpy. She didn’t want to write suck-up stories, which was a lot of what was happening back then. That doesn’t mean she was blacklisted. It’s just that she had a lot of opinions.”
Steven Levy, longtime contributor to WIRED: “I’d push back against the word blacklist—especially [given] the connotations of it, the horrendous things of the McCarthy era. It may very well be that what she was pushing in the core of her writing was an unpopular theme which now people see maybe there was something to it, but back then led to people thinking, we don’t have an appetite for that kind of story.”
John Markoff, tech reporter for the Times until 2016: “There are stories people don’t want to hear. It wasn’t so much about Paulina but that the things she wanted to write didn’t have a market.”
Hafner again: “It was just because she’s Paulina. I mean, it’s hard to be Paulina.”
“I don’t even know if the blacklist existed,” Borsook was saying. “I don’t think it existed.” This time I was the one who’d brought up her years in exile. We were sitting in the shade in her friend’s backyard in Berkeley. It was August, and she was waiting to be photographed for this very magazine, the one that had handled her roughly for a time and then, maybe worse, had decided not to handle her at all. The new edition of Cyberselfish was no longer notional. The paperback had arrived in the mail that day, and when she pulled it out of the padded envelope and held that damn book up, it was as if she were displaying an award. Her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, told me that when the Tin House offer came in, Borsook practically squeaked.
“I—this sounds weird—I don’t think TDB was important enough to be blacklisted,” Borsook said. She had come to see her own exile as part of a larger process. No conspiracies or blacklists were needed to render her disposable. “It was such a changed media landscape,” she said. It was more than the media, too. From the vantage of 2026, Cyberselfish reads a little like Borsook’s account of her own encroaching obsolescence—she was describing a campaign, ultimately successful, to root out a whole way of understanding tech. There could be no seeing the dyer’s hand, no perceiving the Dicks in the system, not in the utopia the technolibertarians were building for us.
Earlier we had been talking about ghosts, the way they seem to pop up in different corners of the story Borsook tells about her life. Even before her friend had shot her, she had this spectral sense of herself, a compulsive feeling of not belonging that only heightened with the violence done to her brain. “Hmm, maybe I really am not supposed to be here,” as she put it in 2013, “and my life ever since has been an accident.” She was standing on a deck now, white hair blowing this way and that in the wind, white scarf wrapped around her neck. A photographer was snapping away, an assistant holding up a bounce board, redirecting daylight toward Borsook’s face. A strange but happy image suggested itself to me: an old ghost in a warm sun.
Does that make any sense?
